title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact
abstract: In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. title: Strengthening AI safety evaluation through independent third-party review
abstract: As frontier AI models grow in capability, so does the importance of ensuring that safety evaluations are rigorous and comprehensive. At Amazon, we invest heavily in internal safety testing for our models, spanning categories like harmful-content generation, cybersecurity risks, privacy protection, and copyright compliance. A core principle of robust quality assurance is that even rigorous internal processes are strengthened by external scrutiny. That's why we partnered with AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute), an independent nonprofit dedicated to third-party evaluation of AI systems, to conduct an independent review of our internal safety evaluation datasets. AVERI’s mandate wasn’t just to test model outputs but to examine the quality and rigor of our tests themselves — asking whether our evaluations stress-test safety boundaries. How the collaboration worked We provided AVERI with a random sample of prompts drawn from our internal safety-evaluation suite. AVERI's team — led by executive director Miles Brundage and including researchers Sean McGregor, A. Feder Cooper, and George Balston — examined the evaluation prompts for diversity, difficulty calibration, and methodological soundness. AVERI assessed the sample independently without input from our evaluation team, ensuring their findings reflected a genuine external perspective. What the review confirmed AVERI’s review validated several strengths of our evaluation process: Comprehensive topical coverage — aligned with publicly documented safety categories including self-harm, cybersecurity, and other risk areas; Diversity of testing approaches — variation in writing style (professional vs. informal), single-turn and multiturn conversations, and original content; Low contamination risk — content that appeared to be original rather than sourced from publicly available datasets, reducing risk of evaluation leakage through pretraining. Opportunities for improvement With any fresh review comes the opportunity to identify areas that internal teams — deeply familiar with their own work — may overlook. AVERI's external perspective surfaced several opportunities to further strengthen an already comprehensive suite: Expanding linguistic and stylistic diversity — While our evaluations include multilingual prompts, AVERI recommended extending multilingual coverage more evenly across risk categories and further varying prompt structures to broaden the range of scenarios tested; Calibrating attack sophistication — AVERI recommended adding more multistep, adversarial prompts to our existing set, so evaluations probe deeper model reasoning and better reflect sophisticated real-world misuse attempts; Maintaining evaluation freshness — AVERI identified a small number of prompts with time-limited references and a few edge cases where grading criteria could be made clearer; Ensuring evaluation signal quality — In some cases, models may refuse based on superficial cues in a prompt, so passing those tests doesn’t necessarily indicate reliable safety behavior in new situations. title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
abstract: Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history. i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2 . This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer. On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results. About i14 i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token. Why linear attention models? Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens. Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O( T 2) to O( T ) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence. Consideration Transformer softmax attention Laplace 3B with GLA Training attention Builds pairwise token scores with O( T 2) scaling Updates chunked recurrent state with O( T ) scaling Inference memory KV cache grows with context Recurrent state remains fixed in size Longer contexts Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation Implementation Uses widely optimized attention kernels Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements. How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2 The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium , because it performed better. The implementation required three changes: Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer. Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times. Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler. The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail. Why AWS Trainium accelerators? AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
abstract: AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet , the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server. With the Smartsheet MCP Server , AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language. In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. Architecture overview The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients. Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right. Figure 1: Smartsheet MCP Server architecture showing MCP client connections from Amazon Quick and Kiro through the server to the Smartsheet API layer Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team: When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard. For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete. Prerequisites Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place: An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro) A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan. A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials

title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions. Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker. Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited. Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself. The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor Figure 1: Domain expertise sits with users while operational data is fragmented across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual. A day in the life A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches. Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes. Figure 2: Traditional multi-tool flow versus a single conversational thread orchestrated by AgentCore Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation. Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?” The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector. Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions” “Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP ( assess_disruption_impact ): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export. Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one” The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP. Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations” The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs. Step 5: Automated follow-up The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”)

title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent). For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both? In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod . We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome. Solution overview This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. The task and dataset The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT). Two metrics matter: Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language? Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language? How SFT and GRPO fit together The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post. The training stack We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO. The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre. title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit. Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500 . Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance , supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary. Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production. Why a foundation, not a feature Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next. So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed. The four tensions Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away. Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant. Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three. Reading content that cannot be trusted. title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
abstract: Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post. Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application. In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done. Models available from Canada With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning. Model Positioning GPT-6.1 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for tasks where both performance and cost matter GPT-6 Astra Complex end-to-end reasoning and agentic tasks GPT-6 Sol Strong reasoning and coding for recurring tasks with economics suited to regular use GPT-6 Luna Fast, low-cost inference for high-volume repeated tasks with adjustable reasoning effort per request GPT-5.6 Sol High reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads GPT-5.6 Terra Balanced performance and cost for everyday production GPT-5.6 Luna Fast and affordable for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide . Cross-Region inference profiles from Canada Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada: US geographic (prefixed us. ) routes requests to your Canadian source Region and US Regions. Choose this profile when your workload requires inference processing to remain within North America (Canada and the US). Global (prefixed global. ) routes requests to supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed. This draws on a broader capacity pool at the time of the request. title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
abstract: Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence. This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime. AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme. This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime , a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script. Solution overview: discover, instantiate, execute The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents. Figure 1: Without AWS Agent Registry (left), endpoints are hardcoded and adding a new agent means code changes plus redeployment. With AWS Agent Registry (right), the orchestrator discovers capabilities through semantic search and new integrations are usable after registration and approval Discover The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path. Instantiate For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the MCPClient . A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material. Execute An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set. Figure 2: End-to-end architecture. A single orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime queries AWS Agent Registry. title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
abstract: When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization. In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK . While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. abstract: In my work with G7–G12 students at Force Academy, a research initiative in Chongqing, I sometimes take a project that appears to be finished and give another student responsibility for using, checking, or modifying it. The handoff is a test of understanding: Can the work still make sense when its creator is no longer there to translate it? The original author knows what every variable means, why a particular decision was made, which tool was used, and which parts can safely be changed. The second student has only what the project makes visible. Generative AI makes the handoff more revealing because it lowers the cost of producing a convincing first version. Students can generate code, analysis, prose, visualizations, and prototypes far more quickly than they could a few years ago. In a classroom, however, a project is useful only insofar as it shows what the student understands and can defend. AI can supply missing code, smooth over incomplete reasoning, or turn a rough idea into fluent prose, so polish is no longer strong evidence of understanding by itself. A concrete example came from a student paper on AI and labor economics, Verification Responsibility in AI-Applicable Occupations. The paper asked what remains economically important when AI makes candidate outputs cheap but a person still has to check those outputs, decide whether they are safe to use, and remain responsible for accepting them. The lead student developed the conceptual model and most of the analytical workflow. A second student was given a narrower job: rerun the main analyses independently, record the versions of the source data, document how occupations in one dataset were linked to occupations in another, and compare the reported tables and figures with the underlying outputs. What looked like procedural verification quickly became a substantive review of the study. The first problem was reproducibility. The analysis ran on the original machine, but too much of the workflow depended on choices that lived in one student’s memory. To reproduce it elsewhere, the team had to record the data transformations, write down the rules for linking occupational datasets, and keep intermediate results so another person could see how the final numbers had been produced rather than simply rerunning a script and trusting the output. The more consequential problem was in the measurement design. An early version of the study used some of the same autonomy and leadership survey items in two different measures: verification responsibility and adaptive capacity. The software had calculated the relationship between those measures correctly, but part of the apparent relationship could have been created by the fact that the two measures shared some of the same inputs. In other words, the code was doing what it had been asked to do; the question was whether the quantities being compared had been defined cleanly enough. The team rebuilt the measures so they no longer shared survey items, removed ambiguous items, and revised the workflow so source versions, cross-dataset links, exclusions, intermediate files, and reported results could be traced. Later versions added alternative specifications and robustness checks. What began as “please rerun this” ended up forcing a redesign of the study. The handoff changed how I read student work. A second user does not merely test whether the files have been packaged neatly; they ask the awkward questions the creator may have stopped noticing. Why is a particular variable there? Which conclusion depends on an assumption that was never made explicit? In this project, those questions reached back into the measurement design. The educational value of the handoff comes from the fact that schoolwork and production software have different ends. Professional developers learn a great deal after software leaves their hands because they have to deliver it, explain it, support it, maintain it, and respond when someone uses it in an unexpected way. title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
abstract: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise. The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down. In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying. The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all. The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access. “Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.” The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science. “One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

title: Here’s the tea
abstract: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s. COURTESY OF MIT GLOBAL HUMANITIES Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s. The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made. “History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
abstract: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn. The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread. “Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.

title: A reason to eat carbs
abstract: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine. This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer. Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were. Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation. This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly. “Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says. Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says. One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them. But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.” Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.”

title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
abstract: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy. Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living. The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says. “Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

title: Taking a swing at a pickleball startup
abstract: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances. He did not. “I spent my early years trying not to get recruited into gangs, getting shot at, watching my friends get murdered, and thinking that if I don’t leave, I will die,” says Anderson, who was raised in Chicago. “I was fortunate to survive.” But he thrived, building an impressive career at the likes of HP, Intel, and the Palo Alto Research Center. Now he is applying his management expertise as CEO of Costa Pickleball, a Las Vegas–based startup that sells high-performance paddles in decorative designs. Beyond giving customers a way to, as he says, “bring their identity to the court,” he is also betting on technology: He’s developing a quieter type of paddle he expects will provide a competitive advantage. Succeeding in today’s pickleball market will be tough, but Anderson thinks he has what it takes, partly thanks to an important lesson he learned at MIT: “There’s nothing you can’t accomplish if you are willing to put effort into it.” Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: A good TA: priceless
abstract: These are images of quizzes I took in 3.091, Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry, in the fall of 1980. One is my very first exam at MIT, and getting 49 out of 100 was a soul-crushing experience. I can still picture the TA, Leszek Pawlowicz, PhD ’87, returning my paper. He had a big smile on his face, and he said something to the effect of “I expect to see you double your score on the next quiz!” Well, I got the message. Studying at MIT was not like studying in high school, but I got 100 on the next quiz and graduated with good enough grades to get me into grad school. All it took, it seems, was that initial kick in the seat of my pants, then a kind hand helping me up off the ground. Recently, I connected with Leszek, and he replied with a charming note. It felt good to let him know how much his encouragement meant to me. A good TA can really have lasting impact! Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
abstract: Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters. Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks to “a providential interaction.” Through MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, she got introduced to cutting-edge x-ray imaging—work she found “really cool.” Now a professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University, she researches galaxy clusters and baryonic matter (matter made of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter) in an effort to learn more about the composition of the universe and its evolution. “Clusters of galaxies are very large scoops of the universe,” says Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020. “It’s like taking a sample from the ocean. If you’re trying to find out the average composition of the ocean’s water, you’d want to study as big a scoop as possible.” Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: A champion for brain injury patients
abstract: Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid the foundation for her life’s work. Today, Totman is a physician specializing in brain injury medicine at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, where she treats adults with head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, and more. She is also the founder of Synapse, a nonprofit focused on providing support for such individuals. The organization grew out of a group she started with Jaclyn Konopka ’14 during medical school at Stanford, and Totman launched it as a national service organization in 2016, while pursuing her master’s degree in public health at Harvard. There are now chapters at 28 universities across the country—and Totman still runs the organization. “There’s a big need for more resources like this,” she says. Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: A cleaner path to rare earth metals
abstract: Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air. “I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste. “The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.” The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables. Read more at www.technologyreview.com/alumni-profiles .

title: Cops raid office of RFK Jr. allies planning “unethical” vaccine trial on babies
abstract: Police in Guinea-Bissau raided the offices of Danish researchers on Monday, seizing doses of hepatitis B vaccine intended for a vaccine trial for newborns. International health experts have called the trial " unethical ," but anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has attempted to fund it with US taxpayer dollars. Under Kennedy, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded the Danish researchers—led by married couple Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project— an unsolicited $1.6 million grant to run the trial . Aaby and Stabell Benn are controversial vaccine researchers who claim vaccines cause overlooked harms. They have been repeatedly praised by Kennedy, but are currently under investigation for alleged scientific misconduct by Danish authorities. Plans for the trial were halted in January as widespread condemnation erupted over the trial's design, which would potentially expose thousands of newborns in the country to hepatitis B, risking a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Outrage flared again after a Rolling Stone story earlier this month claimed the CDC set aside another $1.6 million in funding in late September and planned to move forward with the trial. title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
abstract: We haven't heard many details about Microsoft's upcoming "Project Helix" gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will "play your Xbox and PC games." In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with "a next-generation handheld device" planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800. That future console price range is based on what has "internally been projected" at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if "Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost," the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past . While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore's Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn't as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 . title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
abstract: Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30. Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
abstract: Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn't available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature. As Google points out , a generative AI's outputs are better "when it knows the world and knows you," which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don't have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar. Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around. Read full article Comments

title: OpenBSD 8.0 arrives with security record still intact
abstract: OpenBSD 8.0 is here, marking the project's 61st release and continuing its schedule of semiannual releases dating back to 1996. What started more than 30 years ago as a fork of NetBSD has grown into one of the most security-conscious operating systems in active development. In a post to the project's announcements mailing list, OpenBSD founder Theo de Raadt highlights a host of improvements included with the latest version and writes that the project remains "proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install." The latest OpenBSD version brings new features and improvements across the board. These changes, particularly the new Intel Arc support and expanded virtual address space, should improve compatibility with modern graphics cards and allow the system to map more than 4GB of VRAM . Some of the major updates noted in the release newsletter are as follows: Added support for Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) graphics cards. 512GB kernel virtual address space on AMD64, up from 4GB, allowing VRAM mapping above 4GB. Added hibernation support for ARM64 systems. A new RPKI -to-router daemon: rtrd(8) . RISC-V improvements including kernel support for the 'V' vector extension and support for Advanced Interrupt Architecture. Wireless network driver additions and improvements, including 802.11n and 40 MHz channels for the qwx(4) wireless driver . Added support for up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest virtual machine. Security and internal improvements for LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6 . Improvements to the vmm/vmd virtualization stack . The new OpenBSD also retires support for Loongson architecture after the port stopped working with the Clang 22 compiler. If you're interested in reading over all the changes that come with the new OpenBSD 8.0, you can take a look at the release announcement . Read full article Comments

title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
abstract: Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
abstract: It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation. The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded. The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine. title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
abstract: Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts. The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot , according to The Kyiv Independent . On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety. “This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade's unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.” Read full article Comments

title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
abstract: Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse. Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn't very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we'll need to run complex algorithms, we'd have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit. On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10. Read full article Comments

title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
abstract: In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported . In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy. Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing , its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach" where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents. Read full article Comments

title: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
abstract: The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.” A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster. Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? That’s a question Polestar is trying to answer with researchers at the University of Oxford. Read full article Comments

title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
abstract: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
abstract: As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips. Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit. Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950 . It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars went for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer , but we haven't had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate. title: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
abstract: Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System. The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan's heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. title: 2026년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - JavaScript(ECMAScript)
abstract: 2016년부터 매년 이어 오던 "JavaScript의 동향" 연재는 2020년을 마지막으로 한동안 쉬었습니다. 그사이 6년이 지났고, 그 6년 동안 ECMAScript 명세는 여섯 번 개정되었습니다. 2020년 글을 쓸 때 Stage 2였던 Temporal은 9년에 걸친 논의 끝에 Stage 4에 올랐고, 이제 Chrome과 Firefox, Node.js에서 플래그 없이 쓸 수 있습니다. 달라진 것은 명세만이 아닙니다. 2020년에는 상상하기 어려웠던 방식으로 코드를 쓰는 사람이 늘었습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드의 상당 부분을 작성하고, 사람이 방향을 정하면 AI 에이전트가 브라우저 엔진의 JavaScript 엔진 코드를 다른 언어로 옮기는 일까지 생겼습니다. 2025년 GitHub Octoverse에서 TypeScript가 처음으로 가장 많이 쓰인 언어 1위에 올랐고, GitHub은 그 배경으로 AI를 꼽았습니다. 이번 연재는 다음 네 편으로 구성됩니다. 1편: JavaScript(ECMAScript) 2편: 브라우저 밖의 JavaScript 3편: WebAssembly 4편: 라이브러리와 프레임워크 직전 회차인 2020년과 이후 JavaScript의 동향 - JavaScript(ECMAScript) 에서는 ECMAScript 2020, 2021과 당시 진행 중이던 제안들을 살펴보았습니다. 해마다 발표되는 명세는 'ECMAScript 2026'처럼 연도를 붙여 부르고, 줄여서 'ES2026'이라고도 씁니다. 이 글에서는 먼저 2020년 이후 6년의 공백을 정리하고, 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들이 어떤 결말을 맞았는지 확인합니다. 이어서 TC39 프로세스의 변화, 2026년 6월 승인된 ECMAScript 2026과 2027년 명세에 포함될 기능, 브라우저와 임베디드 엔진의 현황, JavaScript 상표권 분쟁, TypeScript 7을 살펴봅니다. 마지막으로 AI 코딩 도구가 JavaScript와 TypeScript를 쓰는 방식, 그리고 표준을 만드는 방식에 어떤 영향을 주고 있는지 정리합니다. 이 글의 내용은 2026년 10월을 기준으로 작성되었습니다. 글을 읽는 시점에 따라 글의 내용과 사실이 다를 수 있습니다. 2020년 이후 6년 2020년 글은 swyx의 The Third Age of JavaScript 를 인용하며 2020년 이후를 JavaScript의 세 번째 주기로 보았습니다. 이 주기에서는 레거시를 정리하고 도구가 만든 레이어를 걷어 내는 일이 일어날 것이라고 했습니다. 구체적으로는 세 가지를 예상했습니다. CommonJS, AMD 같은 비표준 모듈이 ESM으로 전환될 것입니다. JavaScript 도구가 반드시 JavaScript로 작성될 필요는 없다는 흐름이 강해질 것입니다. TypeScript와 JavaScript가 서로 영향을 주며 함께 발전할 것입니다. 6년이 지난 지금 세 가지 모두 예상한 방향으로 진행되었습니다. 다만 속도와 모습은 예상과 달랐습니다. ESM 전환은 생각보다 오래 걸렸습니다. 전환을 가로막던 가장 큰 장벽은 CommonJS 코드에서 ESM 패키지를 require() 로 불러올 수 없다는 점이었고, 이 문제는 2024년 말이 되어서야 Node.js의 require(esm) 지원으로 풀렸습니다(참고: Node.js 22.12.0 (LTS) ). 인기 npm 패키지의 모듈 형식을 정기적으로 집계하는 wooorm/npm-esm-vs-cjs 데이터에 따르면, ESM을 제공하는(ESM 전용이거나 ESM과 CommonJS를 함께 제공하는) 패키지 비율은 2021년 8월 7.8%에서 2024년 11월 25.9%, 2026년 6월 38.0%로 늘었습니다. 다만 2025년 12월부터 집계 대상 목록의 출처가 바뀌어 그 이전 수치와 바로 비교하기는 어렵습니다. Anthony Fu (Vue, Vite, Nuxt 코어 팀원이자 Vitest, Slidev, UnoCSS 제작자)는 2024년 말 수치를 근거로 새 패키지는 ESM 전용으로 내자고 제안하기도 했습니다(참고: Move on to ESM-only ). 늘어난 것은 분명하지만 여전히 인기 패키지의 60% 이상은 ESM을 제공하지 않습니다. 그림 1 2021~2026년 인기 npm 패키지의 모듈 형식 비율 변화(esm과 dual의 합이 ESM 제공 비율, 출처: wooorm/npm-esm-vs-cjs ) 도구의 언어 전환은 예상보다 빨랐습니다. 2020년 글에서 Babel과 비교했던 SWC 외에도 esbuild(Go), Rolldown과 Oxc(Rust), Biome(Rust) 같은 도구가 주류가 되었습니다. 2025년 3월에는 TypeScript 컴파일러 자체를 Go로 옮기겠다는 발표가 나왔고, 2026년 7월 Go 기반의 TypeScript 7.0이 정식 출시되었습니다(참고: A 10x Faster TypeScript , Announcing TypeScript 7.0 ). 이 글에서는 언어와 런타임에 관련된 부분만 짧게 살펴봅니다. TypeScript는 '보편화'를 넘어 사실상 기본값이 되었습니다. Next.js, Astro, SvelteKit 같은 프레임워크가 프로젝트를 TypeScript로 생성하고, Node.js와 Deno, Bun 모두 .ts 파일을 별도 변환 없이 실행합니다. 예상하지 못한 변화도 있었습니다. 2020년 글은 AI에 대해 한 줄도 쓰지 않았습니다. 그러나 2026년 현재 JavaScript 생태계의 변화를 설명할 때 AI 코딩 도구를 빼놓기 어렵습니다. 이 내용은 "AI 도구로 인한 변화" 절에서 따로 정리합니다. 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들의 결말 2020년 글의 "새로운 또는 완료되지 않은 제안들" 절에서 다룬 제안들은 다음과 같은 결말을 맞았습니다. 표 1 2020년 글에서 소개한 제안들의 현재 상태 제안 2020년 7월 2026년 10월 비고 Top-level await Stage 3 ES2022 2021년 5월 Stage 4 Class fields, private methods, static class features Stage 3 ES2022 2021년 Stage 4 KV Storage 모듈 중단 비활성 브라우저 벤더의 투자 없음 Pipeline Operator Stage 1 Stage 2 2021년 8월 Hack 스타일로 Stage 2 Records & Tuples Stage 1 철회 2025년 4월 철회, Composites로 이어짐 Temporal Stage 2 Stage 4 2026년 3월 Stage 4, ES2027 포함 예정 2020년 글에서 Stage 3에 머물러 있다고 했던 클래스 필드 관련 제안 세 개는 2021년 Stage 4에 올라 ES2022에 포함되었습니다(참고: 2021년 4월 회의록 ).
